title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: The Mill, the Flood, and Family Bonds

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to take George Eliot's great novel apart — passage by passage, character by character — and put it back together again.
A novel about memory, about the hunger of a brilliant girl in a world that has no place for her, about the terrible pull of family — and about a river that never quite lets anyone go.
Three remarkable readers are joining me today, and I want to introduce them properly.
Oliver Trevelyan has given voice to more classic novels on audio than almost anyone alive.
He approaches fiction as a performer first — he hears the comic timing, the grotesque energy, the moments that were written for the voice.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose critical instincts were formed on Johnson, Burke, and a lifetime spent with the great English novelists.
For Edmund, a novel stands or falls on its moral imagination — on what it reveals about character tested by circumstance.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads novels as documents of class power — as anatomies of the systems that shape, constrain, and sometimes crush the people inside them.
He believes great novelists were more radical than they themselves knew, and he makes a compelling case.
We're beginning today with education — specifically, with how Tom Tulliver is being educated, and what that tells us about the world this novel inhabits.
Oliver, Mr Stelling and his methods — where do you want to begin?
The Stelling passages are among the funniest things in the novel, and I think they're funny in a very specific way — the comedy is doing serious work.
Eliot gives us this magnificent image — Mr Broderip's beaver, building his dam in a room up three flights of stairs in London, with no water and no possible progeny.
The beaver's function, you see, is simply to build.
The absence of water is merely an inconvenient accident.
And then the transition — and it is a perfect transition —
"With the same unerring instinct Mr Stelling set to work at his natural method of instilling the Eton Grammar and Euclid into the mind of Tom Tulliver."
The word "instinct" is the blade — the same word that governs the beaver now governs the schoolmaster.
Stelling is not a villain — he's something far more devastating in Eliot's world: he is a man of complete and comfortable certainty.
Oliver is right to identify the satirical precision — but I'd want us to hold on to something that could easily be missed.
Eliot's narrator is not simply mocking Stelling.
There is a rather chilling generosity in the observation that Stelling had no secret belief that everything was humbug.
He believed in religion, in Aristotle, in deaneries — as, Eliot tells us, a Swiss hotel-keeper believes in the beauty of the scenery.
That is a devastating simile, but it is a morally nuanced one.
Stelling is not corrupt — he is merely incurious.
And in Eliot's moral universe, incuriosity about those in your care is its own form of failure.
What Edmund calls incuriosity, I would call structural inevitability.
Stelling is not a one-off failure — he is the product of a system in which the content of education is entirely disconnected from the needs of the people receiving it.
The Eton Grammar and Euclid are not chosen because they educate Tom Tulliver — they are chosen because they mark the class position of the man who teaches them.
And Eliot is precise about this — Stelling's belief in his method was not biased by excessive accuracy or extent of his own scholarship.
The man didn't even know the subject particularly well.
He had the credential, the position, the institution behind him — and that was entirely sufficient.
That is not incuriosity — that is class power operating exactly as it was designed to.
Daniel, I don't want to simply capitulate — but the passage that follows does rather support your reading.
Because what Eliot then does is extraordinary — she shows us exactly what Tom can do.
He can predict with accuracy what number of horses are cantering behind him.
He can throw a stone right into the centre of a given ripple.
He can draw almost perfect squares on his slate without any measurement.
But none of this counts — because none of it can be made to appear on the page of an Eton Grammar.
And then Eliot fires off this extraordinary rhetorical flourish — listen to this —

"O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being 'the freshest modern' instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence, with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without metaphor"
She addresses Aristotle directly.
She is that confident — and that amused.
There is something in that passage which I think resists Daniel's reading, however — and it matters.
Eliot's narrator does not say that Tom's practical intelligence is simply suppressed by the system.
She says, with real care, that his perceptive powers were not at all deficient — indeed, they were quite as strong as those of the Rev. Mr Stelling.
But she also shows us the limits of Tom's mind — the abstractions hideously symbolised in the pages of the Eton Grammar are genuinely beyond him.
This is not simply a story of a good mind crushed by a bad system.
It is a story of the genuine tragedy of wrong fit — a particular mind, a particular method, and no one with the imagination to bridge them.
I take Edmund's point — and I'd never reduce Tom to a simple victim.
But I want to move us to the moment when Tom first encounters Philip Wakem — because something very uncomfortable happens there.
Tom looks at Philip and sees — first and foremost — the hump.
He has a vague notion that the deformity of Wakem's son had some relation to the lawyer's rascality.
And then Eliot gives us his evidence base — and it is this:

"There was a humpbacked tailor in the neighbourhood of Mr Jacobs's academy, who was considered a very unamiable character, and was much hooted after by public-spirited boys solely on the ground of his unsatisfactory moral qualities."
Public-spirited boys.
That is Eliot's irony at its most precise — the cruelty of children dressed up as civic virtue.
Tom is not an individual monster — he has simply absorbed exactly what his world has taught him about bodies that don't conform.
And yet — and this is what I love about this scene — Tom cannot quite make Philip fit the mould he's prepared for him.
The face is not disagreeable.
The brown hair waves and curls at the ends like a girl's — Tom finds that "truly pitiable," which is a very Tom response.
And Philip handles his pencil in an enviable manner.
Curiosity wins, finally — Tom suddenly walks across and looks over Philip's paper.
And then Philip disarms him entirely — with the Greeks.
He tells Tom, with a quite naked enthusiasm, what he would have wished to be.

"I should like to have been a Greek and fought the Persians, and then have come home and have written tragedies, or else have been listened to by everybody for my wisdom, like Socrates, and have died a grand death."
The narrator adds, in parentheses, that Philip was not without a wish to impress the well-made barbarian with a sense of his mental superiority.
"The well-made barbarian" — that parenthetical is worth pausing on.
It is gently mocking of Philip's vanity — but it also tells us exactly how Philip sees the world.
Mind against body — the crippled scholar against the healthy, uncomplicated boy.
This is a rivalry being established — one that will carry enormous weight as the novel develops.
A well-made barbarian — I think that phrase will stay with us for the rest of the episode.
We've seen Tom measured — and found wanting — by a system that can't read him.
And we've seen Philip — who can read everything — sizing up the boy who can't quite see him clearly yet.
Coming up, we turn to the world beyond the schoolroom — to the Dodson family, to Maggie's fierce inner life, and to what it costs to be the wrong kind of intelligent in St Ogg's.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the great currents of George Eliot's novel — its world of commerce, family debt, and provincial life.
Now we go deeper into the characters themselves — into the children at the heart of the book.
Maggie and Tom Tulliver: two young people shaped by the same household, pulled toward entirely different destinies.
With me today are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has given voice to more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive, and he hears Eliot's prose the way a conductor hears a score.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the close moral intelligence of a lifetime spent with great literature — he reads character as destiny.
And Dr Daniel Rosen reads every scene of childhood as a social document — asking what the world does to these young people before they can resist it.
Let's begin with Maggie — and with one of the novel's most quietly devastating little portraits of a child under pressure.
What Eliot does with Maggie's jealousy over Lucy is one of her great comic-tragic strokes — and it hits hardest when you hear it aloud.
There's a moment where the narrator steps in and tells us exactly what is happening inside this small, furious child.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
A white mouse — that is exactly right.
Lucy is so blond and gentle and unthreatening that harming her would be simply monstrous — like cruelty to a small domestic animal.
But then Tom walks in, and suddenly Lucy stops being a creature to be petted and becomes a rival.
And Maggie is actually contemplating slapping and pinching her — specifically because it might vex Tom.
Eliot doesn't flinch from that — she writes it with complete honesty, and somehow with complete sympathy at the same time.
What strikes me in that passage is how precisely Eliot locates the moral life inside a very small emotional event.
Maggie is not a bad child. She is a child with a rich, ungoverned inner life — and no adequate outlet for it.
The jealousy is real. But what makes it tragic rather than simply unpleasant is that Maggie herself knows it is wrong.
That inward knowledge — that awareness of one's own worst impulse — is precisely the beginning of moral character in Eliot's understanding.
And it connects directly to that later scene — when Tom has fainted and Maggie shakes him desperately on the floor.
Eliot gives us the sentence that unlocks everything she feels for her brother.
"She couldn't sorrow yet that he had hurt his foot; it seemed as if all happiness lay in his being alive."
The petty jealousy of the earlier scene and this absolute love are not contradictions. They are the same intensity, turned in different directions.
I'd agree with Edmund on the intensity — but I want to ask what that intensity is pressing against.

Maggie's love for Tom is absolute. And Tom consistently fails to meet it — not because he is cruel by nature, but because the world is already forming him into something that cannot receive what she offers.
Which brings me to Tom at Stelling's — because what happens to him there is a kind of making and unmaking happening simultaneously.
Eliot tells us Tom becomes, under this vigorous treatment, more like a girl than he had ever been in his life.
And then — in one of the most quietly extraordinary moments in the novel — he adds a petition to his evening prayers.
"And please to make me always remember my Latin."
That is not comedy. That is a child being broken by an educational apparatus that was built for someone else entirely.
Latin and Euclid are the currency of a class Tom was never born into. And the school extracts from him exactly what it cannot give back.
Daniel is right that it's devastating — but I have to defend Eliot's comedy here, because it is doing enormous work.
The prayer for Latin is funny — properly, painfully funny — precisely because it reveals the child's desperation in the most innocent possible form.
And then he pauses to consider — Eliot actually gives us Tom pausing — to work out how you pray about Euclid.
The earnestness is complete. The gap between what Tom needs and what prayer can deliver — that's where the tragedy lives.
And notice what Eliot says immediately before that prayer: Tom was not given to hypothesis and experiment.
That phrase could be a criticism. But Eliot deploys it without contempt — it is simply an accurate account of his nature.
Tom's virtues — his firmness, his loyalty, his practical clarity — are genuine virtues. They are simply the wrong instruments for the world Mr Stelling represents.
There is something of Mr Tulliver's predicament here, actually. The man who found himself borrowing from Wakem's client despite every intention to the contrary.
Eliot reaches for an extraordinary comparison when she describes his situation.
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
Oedipus! For a Lincolnshire miller. The comedy of the comparison is intentional — but the tragedy underneath it is entirely real.
The Tullivers are people to whom things happen. Their will is genuine, but external fact is stronger — Eliot says so directly.
That Oedipus comparison is doing something quite specific, I think. It frames the Tullivers as tragic in the classical sense — but Eliot is also winking at us.
Because Oedipus was brought down by fate. Mr Tulliver is brought down by a credit market and an enemy solicitor.
The machinery looks like destiny. But it has very identifiable moving parts — and they all have names.
Which is why Philip Wakem matters so much — because Philip carries that name but refuses to be reducible to it.
There's that question Philip puts to Maggie — one of the most nakedly vulnerable things any character says in the entire novel.
"Maggie, if you had had a brother like me, do you think you should have loved him as well as Tom?"
He is asking whether deformity disqualifies him from the kind of love she gives Tom freely and unconditionally.
That is not a sentimental question. That is the question of a person who has learned precisely where the world places him.
And Philip's confession to Maggie — what he says he will carry forward from their friendship — is equally remarkable to perform.
He tells her — and you have to hear how simply and directly he says it — he tells her what she will mean to him when he is unhappy.
"I'm very fond of you, Maggie; I shall never forget you.
And when I'm very unhappy, I shall always think of you, and wish I had a sister with dark eyes, just like yours."
Dark eyes, just like yours. There is nothing rhetorical about that. It is a child saying the absolute truth of what he feels.
And Eliot trusts it completely. She doesn't decorate it. She doesn't explain it. She just lets it stand.
There's something in all of this — the jealousy, the prayer, the deformity, the dark eyes — that points toward what the novel is really building.
These children are being shaped — by family, by school, by class, by one another — into people who will one day have to reckon with the world as adults.
And Eliot has made us love them so completely by now that the reckoning already feels like loss.
We'll be back shortly to look at the wider world the Tullivers inhabit — the St Ogg's society that surrounds and constrains them.

segments.title: The Machinery of Ruin: Class, Debt, and Dislocation

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been circling the Tulliver household, watching the storm gather — and now we want to look at the machinery underneath.
The debt, the law, the class pressures that grind this family down — and what those pressures reveal about character.
With me as always: Oliver Trevelyan, who hears every sentence in the novel as it was meant to be performed.
Sir Edmund Leigh, whose Oxford-trained eye goes straight to the moral imagination at the heart of the story.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen, who will not let us forget that behind every family quarrel is a structure of economic power.
Daniel, I want to start with you — because George Eliot, before we see a single bill of ruin, does something very strange with Tom Tulliver's face.
Yes — and it's worth pausing on that, because the passage is doing something more unsettling than it first appears.
Tom is introduced as utterly generic — one of those lads who look, as Eliot puts it, as much alike as goslings at twelve or thirteen years of age.
But then the narrator springs the trap.
She tells us that Nature has — and I want to read this precisely —
"the deep cunning which hides itself under the appearance of openness, so that simple people think they can see through her quite well."
Nature conceals her most rigid, inflexible purposes beneath exactly the faces that seem to carry none.
What Eliot is encoding from the very start is a warning: the pink-and-white ordinary boy will become the instrument of the family's social tragedy.
His inflexibility isn't personal — it is structural. It is what this class, at this moment in English history, requires of its men.
And Eliot delivers that warning with such gleeful irony — the prose itself performs the trick it's describing.
She seems to be doing a light comic sketch of a boy — cream and roses, indeterminate nose — and you're almost charmed by him.
Then she pulls the rug away.
She tells us, with this wonderful deadpan, that under such faces she conceals —
"some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most unmodifiable characters."
That triple repetition — rigid, inflexible, unmodifiable — is not careless. It is a rhetorical hammer blow, dressed up as a casual observation.
When I read that aloud, I feel the weight of everything that is going to happen to Maggie pressing down behind those three words.
I think we ought to be careful, though, about reading Tom purely as a social function.
What the passage establishes is something more classical: the inscrutability of character — the idea that we cannot read the inner life from the outer surface.
That is a very old moral claim. It is almost Augustinian.
What Eliot is warning us against is the complacency of surface reading — in life as much as in fiction.
And that warning applies equally to Tom's strengths and to his failures. He is not a villain constructed by class. He is a human being of limited but genuine moral seriousness.
I don't disagree about the moral seriousness — but I think the novel is quite precise about how that seriousness expresses itself.
Take Mr Tulliver's obsession with Wakem. The narrator is absolutely scathing about it, and absolutely clear-eyed about why.
Tulliver's hatred of Wakem is presented as irrational — but the novel shows us it is also a displaced form of class fury.
Wakem is the attorney — the man who knows how to manipulate the law in ways Tulliver cannot access and cannot counter.
The narrator gives us Tulliver's inner voice directly, and listen to how it sounds —
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber, — always looking so sure of his game!"
That's not just prejudice. That's the vocabulary of a man who knows he is being beaten by a system he was never equipped to navigate.
And what a line it is to say aloud. "Cool as a cucumber." The sheer indignation in it.
Eliot has such perfect pitch for the rage of a man who believes absolutely in his own rightness and cannot understand why the world won't confirm it.
And then — this is the comic genius — she gives him the counterpart in Gore, the bald, round-featured man with bland manners and fat hands.
Tulliver's own lawyer is patently inadequate, and Tulliver half-knows it — which makes the whole enterprise even more heartbreaking and more absurd simultaneously.
There is a parallel comedy — if that's not too strong a word — in the passage about Mrs Glegg and the repaid debt.
Mrs Glegg has arranged herself in full magnanimity, anticipating a reconciliation. She has, in her own mind, triumphed.
And then Tulliver's letter arrives, informing her — quite curtly — that he will repay the five hundred pounds within the month.
The narrator tells us he writes that — and I shall read it as Tulliver must have intended it —
"she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
The pride in that sentence is magnificent — and fatal. It is the pride of a man who would rather lose everything than suffer a woman of the Dodson family to think she has him at advantage.
That is a moral failure — but it is recognisably human, and Eliot asks us to understand it, not merely condemn it.
But notice what that pride costs. It is not abstract. That letter is the fulcrum on which the family's ruin tips.
And the novel is very precise about the concatenation of forces. There's a wonderful passage about Mrs Tulliver's influence on her husband's decision to go to law.
The narrator says her pleading might be compared to —
"that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
But then — this is the brilliant, lawyerly move — Eliot immediately redirects blame toward the accumulated weight of all the feathers already in place.
The camel's back was already catastrophically laden. The social and economic pressures had been building for years. Mrs Tulliver is the occasion, not the cause.
Eliot is making a structural argument about causation, wrapped in comic metaphor.
It's a very funny passage — until you realize it isn't, quite.
The camel-and-feather image starts as a wry domestic comedy about a nagging wife, and it's written with enormous comic élan.
But Daniel is exactly right — underneath it is a pretty devastating account of how forces accumulate until one small thing tips a life into catastrophe.
And Eliot is at her most dangerous when she's being most amusing.
All of which brings us, I think, to the scene between Maggie and Tom — which is where the novel's most searching moral argument is delivered.
Maggie's speech to Tom is one of the great pieces of moral rhetoric in Victorian fiction.
She is in the wrong — she acknowledges that freely. But she sees something in Tom that he cannot see in himself.
She tells him —
"You have no pity; you have no sense of your own imperfection and your own sins. It is a sin to be hard; it is not fitting for a mortal, for a Christian."
The charge is devastating — and it is delivered with absolute moral authority, by a character who is simultaneously in disgrace.
That is Eliot's extraordinary achievement here: Maggie is wrong in conduct and right in vision, simultaneously.
And the speech connects directly to what Eliot says, in the narrator's own voice, about moral judgment and maxims.
Tom is the man of maxims made flesh. He has his rules, his categories, his ledger of right and wrong — and they are, within their own terms, perfectly consistent.
But the narrator is unsparing about what such consistency costs.
She writes —

"the mysterious complexity of our life is not to be embraced by maxims, and that to lace ourselves up in formulas of that sort is to repress all the divine promptings and inspirations that spring from growing insight and sympathy."
That word lace — lace ourselves up — is perfect. It suggests both propriety and constriction. The corset of respectability.
Tom's inflexibility is the inflexibility of a class that has decided its own virtues are the measure of all virtue.
And Maggie sees through it — which is precisely why she cannot survive within it.
That line she throws at Tom — "You are nothing but a Pharisee" — lands like a stone in still water.
And she isn't finished. She goes further —
"You have not even a vision of feelings by the side of which your shining virtues are mere darkness!"
Shining virtues — mere darkness. It's magnificent in the mouth. The paradox hits you in the chest before your brain has had time to process it.
Tom would win this argument in any court of public opinion. And Maggie still wins it on the page. That's what makes this novel devastating.
And that gap — between what a society can recognise as virtue and what a novel can hold in view — feels like the centre of everything we've been discussing today.
The debt, the law, the family pride, Tom's rigid code — all of it converges on Maggie, who sees most clearly and suffers most completely.
We'll return in the next segment to the question of what — if anything — Eliot offers as a way through.

segments.title: Eliot's Comic Voice: Irony and Intimacy in Narration

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, a close reading of George Eliot's great novel of childhood, ambition, and the slow violence of provincial life.
I'm your host, and today we're gathered around one of the novel's most distinctive and underrated pleasures: Eliot's comic voice.
The irony, the intimacy, the way the narrator seems to be whispering a shared joke directly into your ear.
Joining me today are three guests who bring very different lenses to Eliot's prose.

Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than almost anyone living, and he reads Eliot the way a musician reads a score — for timing, texture, and the comic breath between the notes.
Sir Edmund Leigh spent decades at Oxford attending to the moral imagination of Victorian fiction, and he brings to Eliot a patient, searching eye for character and conscience.
And Dr Daniel Rosen reads the novel as an anatomy of class and power — asking always who the comedy flatters and who it costs.
Oliver, let's begin with you — and with Maggie in the mill.
The mill passage is one of those places where Eliot is doing something almost impossibly delicate — she's being funny and tender at the same time, and neither one undercuts the other.
There's this extraordinary build-up — the din, the motion, the fine white powder over everything — and then she lands on this beautifully simple sentence.
"the mill was a little world apart from her outside everyday life."
Now that's a sentence written for the voice — the rhythm falls exactly right, and that word "apart" carries all of Maggie's longing.
But then — and this is where Eliot cannot help herself — we get the spiders.
Maggie wonders whether the mill spiders have relatives outside — and whether a floury spider might suffer at a cousin's table where the fly was, as Eliot puts it, au naturel.
It is absolutely absurd — and absolutely true to how an intelligent, solitary child thinks.
Oliver is right that the comedy is inseparable from the tenderness — but I'd go further and say it's inseparable from the characterisation.
The spider speculation isn't simply a joke inserted by the narrator — it's Maggie's joke, rendered by a narrator who loves her.
That distinction matters enormously.
We are being invited not to laugh at Maggie but to share her particular quality of mind — its range, its playfulness, its refusal to be bounded by the merely practical.
This is, I think, what Eliot's irony does at its finest — it discloses character from the inside, as it were, rather than exposing it from without.
I'll agree with both of you — up to a point.
The tenderness is real, and the comedy is genuinely funny.
But notice what's also happening here — Maggie goes to the mill to talk with Luke, the millhand, because she wants him to think well of her understanding, as her father did.
The mill is her refuge, yes — but it's a refuge she can only enter on terms set by men whose approval she craves.
Eliot's comic warmth is not naive — but it can soften the edges of a social constraint that deserves to be felt more sharply.
Daniel's point is well taken — but for pure comic craft, I want to bring in Bob Jakin, because Bob is one of the great comic performances in Victorian fiction.
He's a pedlar, and he's selling Mrs Glegg a piece of figured muslin — and the pitch he runs on her is a masterpiece of reverse psychology.
The whole point is that he tells her not to look at it — it's far too good for the likes of her to even contemplate.
"You might as well look at poor folks's victual, mum; it 'ud on'y take away your appetite."
The dialect spelling, the rhythm, the sheer cheek of it — this is written to be heard, not seen.
Eliot loves Bob the way Dickens loves his great comic grotesques — but with a cleaner eye for how his charm actually operates.
Bob Jakin is one of the novel's most interesting characters precisely because he resists the categories we might reach for.
He is quick-witted, loyal, morally serious in his own fashion — and his comic exuberance is not in tension with those qualities but expressive of them.
What Eliot gives us in the muslin scene is character in action — the pleasure of watching a genuinely quick mind at work.
Bob is delightful — I won't argue otherwise.

But the joke only works because Mrs Glegg's snobbery is so well established — she's the perfect mark, because she cannot bear to think that something fine might be destined for a huckster's wife at Fibb's End.
Eliot's comic irony here is genuinely double-edged — we're laughing at Mrs Glegg's vanity while also recognising that Bob has turned class anxiety into a sales technique.
That's not a comfortable laugh — or shouldn't be.
And then there's the moment Eliot deploys the shortest possible weapon — a single sentence, a rhetorical question, standing entirely alone at the opening of a chapter.
"Had anything remarkable happened?"
That's the entire paragraph.
It's the narrator catching you by the lapels and absolutely refusing to be solemn about the machinery of fiction.
Sterne would have approved.
That intimacy between narrator and reader is something Eliot deploys with great care throughout the novel.
One might call it a kind of narrative contract — the reader is trusted to be an intelligent co-conspirator rather than a passive recipient.
The single-sentence chapter opening is a comic gesture, yes — but it's also an assertion of that contract.
Now, the irony turns much darker — and much more savage — when we come to the passage about Maggie's return to St Ogg's.
This is where the comedy becomes something close to fury.
The narrator invents this figure — the world's wife — and gives her the most devastating mock-tribute imaginable.
"The world's wife, with that fine instinct which is given her for the preservation of Society, saw at once that Miss Tulliver's conduct had been of the most aggravated kind."
"Fine instinct." "Preservation of Society." Every word is a stiletto.
The voice is perfectly reproduced — the tut, the nod, the righteous flush — and then Eliot quietly slides a knife between its ribs.
This passage is where Eliot's comic method reveals its full political reach.
The world's wife is not an individual character — she is ideology speaking in the first person plural.
And what she's protecting is not morality — it's property, reputation, and the marriage market.
Look at how Stephen Guest is treated — a young man of five-and-twenty, not to be too severely judged — while Maggie, who is the injured party, is described as designing and bold.
The irony exposes the double standard with surgical precision — but Eliot also makes you feel the weight of what Maggie actually bears under that standard.
I think one must acknowledge that this is among the most accomplished passages of sustained ironic prose in the Victorian novel.
The final sentence in particular — where the narrator observes that God, unlike the world's wife, had not the care of Society on His hands — is delivered with a perfectly controlled contempt.
And yet I would also say that the passage works because it does not merely satirise — it grieves.
Eliot's irony is never cold — it is always in the service of a genuine moral distress at what is being done to a human being.
And that's the thread that runs from the spiders in the mill to the world's wife in St Ogg's — the narrator is always on the side of the person who thinks too much for the world she's been given.
There's also a marvellous moment where Philip Wakem, of all people, delivers a line of almost operatic disdain to his father.
"You know best what satisfaction you would have, beyond that of gratifying a ridiculous rancor worthy only of wandering savages."
Philip is gentle, damaged, frequently passive — and then he produces that.
The comic timing is perfect — the long build of Philip's suffering, and then the sudden, precise contempt.
What strikes me listening to all of this is that Eliot's comic voice is never a separate register from her moral voice — they're the same instrument, played with different pressure.
The spiders, the muslin, the world's wife — they're all performing the same fundamental act of close, loving, fierce attention to human life.
We'll be back shortly to look at how the novel handles the pressures of family, memory, and the past that will not stay buried.

segments.title: The Weight of Circumstance: Desire Against Social Law

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're exploring how Maggie Tulliver's hunger — for knowledge, for escape, for belonging — runs headlong into everything her world will and won't permit.
With me, as always, are our three remarkable guides to this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the most attentive reader of voices this novel could hope for.
Sir Edmund Leigh — Oxford don and moral critic, who reads every novel as a test of character under pressure.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen — cultural historian, who finds in Maggie's thwarted ambitions an anatomy of class and power.
Oliver, let's start with the scene that launched a thousand childhood memories — Maggie's decision to run away to the gypsies.
It's one of the great comic set-ups in Victorian fiction, and Eliot plays it with perfect timing.
The resolution doesn't build gradually — it arrives in a single magnificent sentence.
Listen to how she puts it:
"No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more."
That exclamation mark does all the work — Maggie has already had the argument with herself, and she's won it.
And then — this is the masterpiece — Eliot adds that this was "by no means a new idea."
The escape plan Maggie presents as her great crisis has been sitting in her back pocket for months.
What strikes me is less the comedy than the loneliness underneath it.
Maggie doesn't simply want to run away — she wants, as Eliot puts it, to be "entirely in harmony with circumstances."
That is a child's formulation of a lifelong problem.
She will spend the entire novel searching for a circumstance that fits the shape of who she is.
And she will not find one.
Edmund is right about the loneliness, but I want to press on what it means that the gypsies are the fantasy.
Maggie has been told she is "half wild" — that's the language of social exclusion turned into a label.
She doesn't flee to luxury or to a higher class — she flees toward the most marginalised people in England.
And crucially, she imagines they will receive her with respect because of her "superior knowledge."
Intelligence is the only currency Maggie possesses — and in St Ogg's it buys her nothing.
And then Eliot demolishes the fantasy with one of the most carefully constructed comic passages I know.
She gives us this portrait of Maggie's education — or rather, her magnificent non-education.
The line is extraordinary:
"in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
"Small mind" — and yet it is vast, because it's full of things nobody thought to put there.
She knows "polygamy" and has deduced what "poly" means from first principles.
But she has no idea that gypsies might be short of groceries.
Eliot describes Maggie's thoughts as "the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams."
That phrase is not merely comic — it is the whole tragedy of Maggie in miniature.
Her acumen she cannot deploy because no institution will receive it.
Her blind dreams she cannot surrender because they are all she has to keep her alive.
And then the fantasy collapses into something much darker, and I think Eliot is precise about the mechanism.
When Maggie actually sits among the gypsies, her mind doesn't simply correct itself — it spirals.
The passage is almost gothic in its acceleration:
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"Gradual cooking" — Eliot refuses to let us forget this is still a child's mind.
But the terror is real, and it comes from the collapse of the only narrative that made her predicament bearable.
I love that she worries most not about being eaten, but about offending the gypsies by letting them see her opinion of them.
Even in mortal terror, Maggie's social anxiety is perfectly intact.
And then Eliot gives us this magnificent aside — she wondered whether the Devil, if really present, would know her thoughts.
"with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded."
That's a joke — but it's also a portrait of a mind that cannot stop reasoning even when it should simply run.
That irrepressible reasoning mind — it carries into Maggie's encounter with Tom's schoolbooks.
Edmund, the Latin Grammar passage is one I know you've returned to many times — what does it reveal about Maggie?
It reveals the particular quality of her imagination, which is not merely hungry but genuinely responsive.
Eliot's image is one I find extraordinarily beautiful.
She describes the fragmentary Latin sentences as:
"like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown plants, brought from some far-off region — gave boundless scope to her imagination."
Eliot is telling us that Maggie's mind needs not completion but suggestion — not answers but openings.
That is precisely the kind of mind that the society of St Ogg's has no mechanism for cultivating.
And notice whose Latin Grammar it is — Tom's.
Tom, who is being educated at real expense, with a proper schoolmaster, with Latin and mathematics laid out systematically before him.
Maggie finds the Latin Grammar "quite soothing" — and proceeds to outpace him.
She is proud, Eliot tells us, "because she found it interesting" — as if intellectual pleasure is itself a transgression.
The education that might have saved her is the one that was never on offer.
And she gets lost in "the thick grove penetrable by no star" — which is a quotation within a quotation, a Latin example that opens into pure atmosphere.
And then Tom calls out and she has to stop.
That full stop after "when Tom called out" is doing everything.
The interruption is so ordinary, so inevitable, and so completely crushing.
That pattern of reaching and being called back runs through everything we've discussed.
And it arrives in a moment of real tenderness — Maggie's encounter with Philip Wakem.
Daniel, you've described this scene as one of the most quietly radical moments in the novel.
Because Maggie does something that no other character in the novel manages — she sees past the body.
Not past it as an act of charity, but simply and practically.
She says — and this is verbatim from the text —
"Should you like me to kiss you, as I do Tom? I will, if you like."
The conditional — "if you like" — is everything.
It gives Philip agency, refuses to make the gesture about Maggie's virtue, and treats him as someone with preferences.
It is an act of natural goodness — and I would resist the urge to make it more programmatic than it is.
Maggie is not making an argument about disability or social convention.
She is wondering, as she puts it, how she could convince Philip that she could like him "just as well."
The comparison to Tom is not a diminishment — it is Maggie offering the most precious thing she possesses.
The fact that she gets it from Tom, and Tom is often cold to her — that undercurrent is there, but it need not overwhelm the simple goodness of the gesture.
What moves me is the note of mild regret that precedes it — "I think you're fonder of me than Tom is."
"Rather sorrowfully" — Eliot's adverb.
She registers the truth about Tom without bitterness, and immediately redirects her energy toward Philip.
That's the thing about Maggie — her emotional intelligence is extraordinary, and it perpetually outruns the life available to her.
"The most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge" — and the most unexpected tenderness alongside the most unexpected sorrow.
From a child's furious bolt toward the gypsies to a quiet offer of a kiss — we've traced something very close to the heart of this novel.
In our next segment, we'll follow that hunger further — into the choices Maggie must make as a young woman, and the forces that are already waiting to defeat her.

segments.title: Narrative Atmosphere and the Philosophy of Loss

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we are deep inside George Eliot's great novel of memory, family, and irreversible loss.
This episode brings together three readers whose disagreements are, frankly, as illuminating as their agreements.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than perhaps anyone living — he hears this prose the way a musician hears a score.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the patience and moral seriousness of a lifetime reading fiction as a guide to individual character.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen reads every novel as an X-ray of the social arrangements that produce its characters — their suffering, their choices, their limits.
Our focus in this segment is narrative atmosphere — and what George Eliot does with the philosophy of loss.
Oliver, let's begin with you — because the opening gambit of this novel is one of the most extraordinary things Eliot ever did.
It really is extraordinary — and I mean that as a performer, not just as a reader.
Eliot opens the novel with what feels like pure atmospheric description — the river, the mill, the winter light.
And then — she pulls the rug completely.
She says — and I have to read this because the effect only works in full —

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
She has been asleep in a chair.
The entire opening — this rich, vivid, present-tense world — was a dream.
The loss is built into the structure before the story has even properly begun.
What strikes me is the tact of it — the sheer literary tact.
Eliot could have opened with a chapter heading and a date and been done with it.
Instead she places the reader inside a consciousness that is already mourning — mourning before it can explain what has been lost.
That is an act of moral imagination, not merely technical cleverness.
The benumbed arms — that physical detail of someone who has sat too long in grief-reverie — that is deeply felt.
Eliot wants us to feel the weight of what memory costs the body.
I want to hold on to what Edmund has just said — about mourning before explanation.
Because what the novel then proceeds to show us is precisely what has been lost — and who loses it.
It is the Tulliver family — a provincial milling family — ground down by debt, by law, by the machinery of creditors and cousins.
The dream of the mill is beautiful precisely because the waking reality is dispossession.
And when Tom Tulliver stands before his aunts and pleads the family's case, the stakes are absolutely material.
He says — and the directness of this is almost shocking in the context of Victorian family discourse —
"wouldn't it be better to give it now, and pay the debt we're going to be sold up for, and save my mother from parting with her furniture?"
The furniture — the mother's furniture — stands in for everything that makes a home rather than a ruin.
Tom in that scene is doing something extraordinary for a boy of his age and his emotional vocabulary.
He's essentially appealing to the Dodsons' own values — the primacy of family respectability — and turning those values back on them as an argument for generosity.
It's quite a sophisticated rhetorical move from someone Eliot has already established as having very little imagination.
Which points, rather neatly, to where the novel eventually takes us with Tom.
Because Eliot is devastatingly precise about what Tom's intelligence actually is — and is not.
She writes —
"There was a terrible cutting truth in Tom's words,—that hard rind of truth which is discerned by unimaginative, unsympathetic minds."
A hard rind of truth — not the nourishing fruit of it, but the rind.
That is one of the finest sentences in the novel, and Oliver is right to pause on it.
But I want to resist the reading that makes Tom simply the villain of the piece.
Eliot is doing something more careful than that — she grants him his truth even as she indicts his narrowness.
Maggie, we are told, writhed under his judgment — but she also judged him in return.
Both siblings are partially right and profoundly limited — and that is the moral tragedy, not a social one.
I wouldn't separate the moral and the social quite so cleanly.
Tom's narrowness is not simply a temperamental accident — it has been shaped by everything the novel has shown us about how boys and girls are educated, valued, and constrained.
And the attack on Philip Wakem shows us exactly what Tom's moral code actually serves.
Listen to the language he uses —

"you—you to try and worm yourself into the affections of a handsome girl who is not eighteen, and has been shut out from the world by her father's misfortunes! That's your crooked notion of honour, is it?"
The word handsome is not accidental — Maggie is property to be disposed of correctly, not a person exercising her own will.
Tom's moral code is the code of patriarchal honour, dressed in the language of brotherly love.
And yet Eliot also gives Tom the phrase — and I find this almost unbearable — "what you'd never get by fair means."
Because there is a truth in it — Philip's situation is genuinely compromised, genuinely impossible.
Eliot never lets her villains be purely wrong — which is what makes reading her such uncomfortable, exhilarating work.
That discomfort — that refusal of easy verdict — runs through every level of the novel's construction, as we've been seeing.
We began with a narrator waking from a dream, and we've arrived at Maggie trapped between her brother's hard truth and her own impossible needs.
In our next segment, we'll follow Maggie deeper into that trap — and ask what the novel truly makes of her choices.

segments.title: Drowning Together: The Limits of Human Agency

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the forces that bear down on the Tullivers — legal, educational, familial.
And now we arrive at the ruin itself — the moment when all those forces converge into a single catastrophe.
Oliver, you've been circling this all episode — the comedy that isn't really comedy at all.
Yes, and what I keep returning to is that Eliot earns the tragedy by making you laugh first.
Take Tulliver's theory of the law — which is presented with such deadpan affection.
"Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck and the strongest spurs."
It's glorious nonsense — and Tulliver believes every syllable of it with complete sincerity.
That's the comic trap Eliot sets for us — we're delighted by him just long enough to be devastated when he falls.
And the fall, when it comes, is delivered through Maggie — which is, I think, the most morally precise decision in the novel.
She carries the knowledge her father cannot bear to speak aloud.
Eliot gives her those words at full, terrible velocity — listen to how the sentence breaks open.
"Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and the land and everything; he will have nothing left."
Nothing left. It is the most comprehensive sentence of loss I know in Victorian fiction.
Tulliver loses not property but identity — the mill is who he is.
That identity was never secure, though — and the educational system is partly what ensured it couldn't be.
Eliot is unsparing on how the clerical-educational racket worked against men like Tulliver.
She sets up the argument with savage precision — and then delivers the punchline as a rhetorical question.

"Any of those low callings in which men are obliged to do good work at a low price were forbidden to clergymen; was it their fault if their only resource was to turn out very poor work at a high price?"
The system is self-sealing — it punishes the honest tradesman while protecting the incompetent gentleman.
Tulliver didn't simply make bad decisions — he was operating inside an apparatus designed to destroy him.
And yet he's the one who ends up horizontal, unrecognised by everyone except Maggie.
That detail — that he knows nobody but her — is where Eliot stops being satirical entirely.
She gives Maggie the line simply, without ornament.
"He has known nobody but me ever since — he seems to have lost his senses."
There's nothing to perform there — you just have to say it and step back.
The novel has earned its silence.
What moves me is the particular grammar of that moment — Maggie answers the easy question first.
'He's at home,' she says — and then the pause, and then the devastation.
Eliot understood that grief defers itself — that the mind finds the smaller truth before it can bear the larger.
That is not social observation. That is moral psychology of the highest order.
I won't quarrel with that — but I'd say the psychology and the sociology are inseparable here.
Tulliver's collapse of mind mirrors the collapse of everything he built his identity on.
The cock-fight theory of law, the gamble on Stelling's schooling, the doomed lawsuit — all of it is one continuous wager that the system placed against him.
Eliot doesn't let him off the hook for his stubbornness — but she doesn't let the system off either.
And perhaps that double refusal — to excuse the man, and to excuse the world that made him — is what gives this novel its permanent force.
Oliver, Edmund, Daniel — it has been a genuine pleasure thinking through this novel in your company.
The Mill on the Floss rewards exactly this kind of attention — and more besides.
Thank you for listening to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

c14:p8.text:
Perhaps it was because teaching came naturally to Mr Stelling, that he set
about it with that uniformity of method and independence of circumstances which
distinguish the actions of animals understood to be under the immediate
teaching of nature. Mr Broderip’s amiable beaver, as that charming
naturalist tells us, busied himself as earnestly in constructing a dam, in a
room up three pair of stairs in London, as if he had been laying his foundation
in a stream or lake in Upper Canada. It was “Binny’s”
function to build; the absence of water or of possible progeny was an accident
for which he was not accountable. With the same unerring instinct Mr Stelling
set to work at his natural method of instilling the Eton Grammar and Euclid
into the mind of Tom Tulliver. This, he considered, was the only basis of solid
instruction; all other means of education were mere charlatanism, and could
produce nothing better than smatterers. Fixed on this firm basis, a man might
observe the display of various or special knowledge made by irregularly
educated people with a pitying smile; all that sort of thing was very well, but
it was impossible these people could form sound opinions. In holding this
conviction Mr Stelling was not biassed, as some tutors have been, by the
excessive accuracy or extent of his own scholarship; and as to his views about
Euclid, no opinion could have been freer from personal partiality. Mr Stelling
was very far from being led astray by enthusiasm, either religious or
intellectual; on the other hand, he had no secret belief that everything was
humbug. He thought religion was a very excellent thing, and Aristotle a great
authority, and deaneries and prebends useful institutions, and Great Britain
the providential bulwark of Protestantism, and faith in the unseen a great
support to afflicted minds; he believed in all these things, as a Swiss
hotel-keeper believes in the beauty of the scenery around him, and in the
pleasure it gives to artistic visitors. And in the same way Mr Stelling
believed in his method of education; he had no doubt that he was doing the very
best thing for Mr Tulliver’s boy. Of course, when the miller talked of
“mapping” and “summing” in a vague and diffident
manner, Mr Stelling had set his mind at rest by an assurance that he understood
what was wanted; for how was it possible the good man could form any reasonable
judgment about the matter? Mr Stelling’s duty was to teach the lad in the
only right way,—indeed he knew no other; he had not wasted his time in
the acquirement of anything abnormal.
c14:p8.summary: Eliot compares Stelling's mechanical teaching method to a beaver building a dam regardless of circumstance, criticizing his inflexible adherence to classical education.
c14:p8.best_quote: Mr Stelling set to work at his natural method of instilling the Eton Grammar and Euclid into the mind of Tom Tulliver

c14:p9.text:
He very soon set down poor Tom as a thoroughly stupid lad; for though by hard
labour he could get particular declensions into his brain, anything so abstract
as the relation between cases and terminations could by no means get such a
lodgment there as to enable him to recognise a chance genitive or dative. This
struck Mr Stelling as something more than natural stupidity; he suspected
obstinacy, or at any rate indifference, and lectured Tom severely on his want
of thorough application. “You feel no interest in what you’re
doing, sir,” Mr Stelling would say, and the reproach was painfully true.
Tom had never found any difficulty in discerning a pointer from a setter, when
once he had been told the distinction, and his perceptive powers were not at
all deficient. I fancy they were quite as strong as those of the Rev. Mr
Stelling; for Tom could predict with accuracy what number of horses were
cantering behind him, he could throw a stone right into the centre of a given
ripple, he could guess to a fraction how many lengths of his stick it would
take to reach across the playground, and could draw almost perfect squares on
his slate without any measurement. But Mr Stelling took no note of these
things; he only observed that Tom’s faculties failed him before the
abstractions hideously symbolised to him in the pages of the Eton Grammar, and
that he was in a state bordering on idiocy with regard to the demonstration
that two given triangles must be equal, though he could discern with great
promptitude and certainty the fact that they  were  equal. Whence Mr
Stelling concluded that Tom’s brain, being peculiarly impervious to
etymology and demonstrations, was peculiarly in need of being ploughed and
harrowed by these patent implements; it was his favourite metaphor, that the
classics and geometry constituted that culture of the mind which prepared it
for the reception of any subsequent crop. I say nothing against Mr
Stelling’s theory; if we are to have one regimen for all minds, his seems
to me as good as any other. I only know it turned out as uncomfortably for Tom
Tulliver as if he had been plied with cheese in order to remedy a gastric
weakness which prevented him from digesting it. It is astonishing what a
different result one gets by changing the metaphor! Once call the brain an
intellectual stomach, and one’s ingenious conception of the classics and
geometry as ploughs and harrows seems to settle nothing. But then it is open to
some one else to follow great authorities, and call the mind a sheet of white
paper or a mirror, in which case one’s knowledge of the digestive process
becomes quite irrelevant. It was doubtless an ingenious idea to call the camel
the ship of the desert, but it would hardly lead one far in training that
useful beast. O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being “the
freshest modern” instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have
mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence,
with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without
metaphor,—that we can so seldom declare what a thing is, except by saying
it is something else?
c14:p9.summary: Stelling mistakes Tom's inability to grasp abstract grammar for stupidity, when Tom's perceptual and practical skills are actually exceptional; the narrator critiques the limitations of metaphorical thinking.
c14:p9.best_quote: O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being 'the freshest modern' instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence, with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without metaphor

c16:p7.text:
Tom began to look oftener and longer at Philip’s face, for he could see
it without noticing the hump, and it was really not a disagreeable
face,—very old-looking, Tom thought. He wondered how much older Philip
was than himself. An anatomist—even a mere physiognomist—would have
seen that the deformity of Philip’s spine was not a congenital hump, but
the result of an accident in infancy; but you do not expect from Tom any
acquaintance with such distinctions; to him, Philip was simply a humpback. He
had a vague notion that the deformity of Wakem’s son had some relation to
the lawyer’s rascality, of which he had so often heard his father talk
with hot emphasis; and he felt, too, a half-admitted fear of him as probably a
spiteful fellow, who, not being able to fight you, had cunning ways of doing
you a mischief by the sly. There was a humpbacked tailor in the neighbourhood
of Mr Jacobs’s academy, who was considered a very unamiable character,
and was much hooted after by public-spirited boys solely on the ground of his
unsatisfactory moral qualities; so that Tom was not without a basis of fact to
go upon. Still, no face could be more unlike that ugly tailor’s than this
melancholy boy’s face,—the brown hair round it waved and curled at
the ends like a girl’s: Tom thought that truly pitiable. This Wakem was a
pale, puny fellow, and it was quite clear he would not be able to play at
anything worth speaking of; but he handled his pencil in an enviable manner,
and was apparently making one thing after another without any trouble. What was
he drawing? Tom was quite warm now, and wanted something new to be going
forward. It was certainly more agreeable to have an ill-natured humpback as a
companion than to stand looking out of the study window at the rain, and
kicking his foot against the washboard in solitude; something would happen
every day,—“a quarrel or something”; and Tom thought he
should rather like to show Philip that he had better not try his spiteful
tricks on  him . He suddenly walked across the hearth and looked over
Philip’s paper.
c16:p7.summary: Tom begins to observe Philip's actual face and manner, finding him less disagreeable than expected, though Tom's prejudices about deformity and the Wakem name persist, reinforced by memory of a disagreeable humpbacked tailor.
c16:p7.best_quote: There was a humpbacked tailor in the neighbourhood of Mr Jacobs's academy, who was considered a very unamiable character, and was much hooted after by public-spirited boys solely on the ground of his unsatisfactory moral qualities.

c16:p36.text:
“Oh, I don’t mind,” said Philip, unable to choke a laugh;
“I can remember things easily. And there are some lessons I’m very
fond of. I’m very fond of Greek history, and everything about the Greeks.
I should like to have been a Greek and fought the Persians, and then have come
home and have written tragedies, or else have been listened to by everybody for
my wisdom, like Socrates, and have died a grand death.” (Philip, you
perceive, was not without a wish to impress the well-made barbarian with a
sense of his mental superiority.)
c16:p36.summary: Philip expresses his romantic wish to have been an ancient Greek hero and sage, revealing intellectual idealism and a desire to show Tom his mental superiority.
c16:p36.best_quote: I should like to have been a Greek and fought the Persians, and then have come home and have written tragedies, or else have been listened to by everybody for my wisdom, like Socrates, and have died a grand death.

Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.
c10:p1.summary: Maggie's jealousy transforms her affection into potential cruelty; she blames Lucy for Tom's unkindness and fantasizes about hurting her to vex Tom.
